identified_problem: D2 rated personalised tasks Weak on GenAI exposure and authorship assurance, and only Moderate on capability verification, process visibility and workload. Item-format features explained little of AI resistance, so personalising or contextualising the question is not a security measure [J3], [R73], and personal reflections and portfolios stayed open to AI misuse [S208], [R24]. A personalised artefact does not show who produced it, and marks did not respond to verbatim AI-authored code [R73], [J1].
recommended_redesign: Use personalisation (local context, the student's own dataset or a different topic per student) for authenticity and alignment, not as a security measure [J3], [R15], [R04].
Pair each personalised task with justification and questioning tied to the student's own work, for example short viva questions generated from each submission [S156], [R11], [R24].
Where AI is permitted, give marks for checking AI output against the student's own context for completeness, bias and hallucination, and specify tools that are free to all students [R15], [R20].
Test each task against current GenAI before use, and check that individual versions are of similar difficulty [R73], [R51], [R89].
justification: Finding: in a computing foundation-year module of 88 students, each student chose a different technology and marks covered prompts, AI outputs and a reflection that checked AI output; student satisfaction rose on the previous year, but the only misconduct check relied on detectors the authors call unreliable [R15]. LLM-generated viva questions specific to each project reached QWK 0.782 agreement with human grades for over 250 students [S156], while LLM-generated per-student questions varied in difficulty by up to 30% [R89]. Interpretation: personalisation supports authenticity and alignment, but individual assurance comes from the questioning or justification paired with it, not from the personal content of the task [J3].
implementation_considerations: Cohort size: hand-designed personalised tasks are workable in small cohorts [R94], [R71]. A different topic per student ran with 88 students [R15]. Large cohorts need automated generation or questioning, tested with over 250 students [S156], and platform capacity is a risk, since one platform failed at 300 concurrent users [R89].

Staff time: personalisation shifts work to preparing, calibrating and marking divergent tasks [R24], [S105]. One claim that automated generation cut administrative time by 68% is not supported in that study's results [R89].
Cost: low-tech contextualisation fits existing structures at little cost [R24], while tool-based variants need purpose-built platforms and skills [R71], [R89], [S156].
Equity: calibrate difficulty across versions [R89], expect divided student views on the fairness of AI-resistant tasks [R71], and address free versus premium tool access [R20], [R15].
Durability: resistance that depends on what current models do not know, such as custom commands, is likely to be temporary [R71], [J3].
evidence_status: Partly implemented in computing (components tested separately, not together)
evidence_status_basis: R15 (computing = Y; quality 2/5; 88 students) implemented a divergent, personalised task with marks for prompts, AI outputs and critical reflection, and reported satisfaction and pass outcomes. S156 (computing = Y; quality 5/5; over 250 students in 67 groups) implemented and evaluated submission-specific viva questions against human grading. R89 (computing = Y; quality 2/5) generated a unique question per learner and reported acceptability and difficulty variation, and R94 (computing = Y; quality 1/5; classes up to 30) used randomly drawn topics with a short oral. The components were tested separately; no study measured whether personalised tasks reduce GenAI misuse compared with standard tasks, so the integrity benefit remains untested.
risks_and_limits: Personalisation cannot stop GenAI completing the task, and cosmetic variation adds nothing [J3], [R73]. A personal artefact does not show authorship or how AI was used [J1]. Individual versions may differ in difficulty [R89], automated viva questioning sometimes asked students to repeat answers already given and was not framed as an integrity measure [S156], and no study measured effects for students with disabilities, anxiety or English as an additional language.
